title: The Lord turned and looked (Luke 22:54–71)
hook: at the third denial, Jesus turns and looks at Peter

segments.voice: Yesterday, he touched his ear and healed the man who came to arrest him. Your line was no more of this. What did you start to mend? Day five hundred eighty-two.

They take Jesus to the high priest's house. Peter follows, Luke says, afar off. Close enough to see. Far enough to leave. In the middle of the courtyard someone has lit a fire against the cold night, and people are sitting around it, and Peter sits down with them. Warm hands, firelight on faces. A servant girl looks at him for a long moment and says, this man was with him too. Peter says, woman, I don't know him. A little later someone else: you're one of them. Man, I'm not. About an hour passes. Then a third person is certain: he's a Galilean, he was with him. Matthew adds that his accent gives him away.

Peter answers the third time: man, I don't know what you're saying. And while he's still speaking, the rooster crows. Then comes the line that only Luke has, in the King James words: "And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And Peter went out, and wept bitterly." Luke doesn't say exactly where Jesus is, only that he's close enough to turn and see Peter. Just a few hours earlier, at the table, Jesus told Peter, I have prayed for you, that your faith fail not. Now, across a courtyard, one look. Luke doesn't describe it. He doesn't say angry or sad or kind. He just says the Lord turned and looked. And the look sends Peter out into the night, weeping. Christians have spent centuries imagining that look, in sermons and in paintings. Many hear it as the opposite of a glare: the look of someone who already knew, already prayed, and still hasn't let go of him. Notice too that Peter's tears are the beginning, not the end, of his story. After that, Luke goes on: the men holding Jesus mock him, blindfold him, hit him, and say, prophesy, who struck you? At daybreak the council asks him, are you the Christ? And he answers that if he told them, they wouldn't believe him. The night is long. But Luke wants you to remember one moment from it: a man who just failed three times, and the face he saw when he looked up.
screen: `TEARS ARE NOT THE END FOR PETER.`
then, large: `THE LORD TURNED, AND LOOKED UPON PETER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: imagine a look of love, not blame. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you did that you're ashamed of. Not the worst thing, just something that still stings. Now imagine someone who loves you finding out, and turning to look at you. Most of us imagine a glare. Try instead a face that already knew, and isn't leaving. Stay with that face for a minute. If you pray, you can imagine it as the face of Christ. The bell holds the time.
The Lord turned and looked. Luke's single line at the third denial: no words, only a look across the courtyard, and Peter remembers and weeps.
screen: `THE LORD TURNED AND LOOKED — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the lord looked at peter. Today, when someone lets you down, try to look at them the way you'd hope to be looked at. Day five hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Christians read Peter's denial during Holy Week, and in many churches the rooster has become a symbol of Peter's failure and restoration, sometimes set on top of church steeples.

fork.reveal: he denies it a third time, and while he's still speaking the rooster crows, and the Lord turns and looks at him.

original.note: Greek: he looked into, he fixed his gaze on. Luke's word for Jesus's look at Peter.

trapdoor: what you thought: Peter denies Jesus three times, then feels guilty.
what it means: at the third denial Jesus turns and looks at him, and the look sends Peter out weeping, a failure that is not the end of him.
what a scholar hears: only Luke has the look, and he places Jesus within sight of the courtyard; the verb emblepo means to look straight at someone.

sources.quoted: And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.

notes: Only Luke reports that the Lord turned and looked at Peter (22:61). Confirm.
Rooster on church steeples linked to Peter's denial: common tradition; confirm phrasing in howItsDone.
Ordering: in Luke the denials happen during the night and the council meets at day (22:66), unlike Mark and Matthew. The script follows Luke.
Original ἐνέβλεψεν (aorist of ἐμβλέπω), Luke 22:61. Confirm.
Review edit: the hook's accent detail comes from Matthew 26:73, not Luke (Luke 22:59 says only 'he is a Galilaean'); now attributed to Matthew.
Review edit: Luke does not say Jesus was in the courtyard itself; the teach now says only that he was close enough to turn and see Peter.
Review edit: Luke 22:67 is a statement ('If I tell you, ye will not believe'), not a question; the teach now paraphrases it as such.
